structure.title: Defining poetic action
structure.text: Early chapters distinguish kinds of imitation and establish the components of tragedy, especially the organisation of action.

structure.title: Making and judging plots
structure.text: Later chapters examine reversal, recognition, character, language, and epic. Examples test what makes an invented sequence convincing.

people.name: Imitation
people.text: Aristotle's word for what poetry, drama and painting do: present people acting, which he thinks humans take natural pleasure in from childhood.

people.name: Reversal
people.text: A turn in the plot where an action produces the opposite of what was intended, which Aristotle counts among tragedy's most powerful effects.

people.name: Recognition
people.text: The moment a character learns something that changes everything, which Aristotle thinks works best when it comes at the same time as a reversal.

context.title: Plot as arrangement
context.text: Aristotle is concerned with how events belong together, not merely which events occur. Probability and necessity connect one action to another.
context.takeaway: Ask why this event follows that one.

context.title: Greek tragedy
context.text: Familiarity with one tragedy helps make the examples tangible. The argument remains readable without knowing every lost or surviving play mentioned.
context.takeaway: Examples clarify claims rather than form a reading syllabus.

notice.text: Notice distinctions between history and poetry.
notice.why: Aristotle assigns invention a kind of explanatory reach.

notice.text: Compare rules with the examples that qualify them.
notice.why: The account is more flexible than a list of storytelling commandments.

opening: A messenger arrives with good news, and the news destroys the person it was meant to comfort. Aristotle is interested in how a story can produce a reversal like that without feeling contrived. He studies what makes events belong together, why recognition can hurt, and how an invented action can arouse real pity and fear. His surviving account is compact enough to read quickly, but it keeps returning attention to the difficult craft beneath a story that seems to unfold inevitably.
